newsitem.title: USA: Industry stunned by U.S. energy secretary choice.
newsitem.headline: Industry stunned by U.S. energy secretary choice.

text.p: Energy industry officials were stunned Friday by President Bill Clinton's decision to pick Transportation Secretary Federico Pena as his new energy secretary.

White House officials had said Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chairwoman Elizabeth Moler was the top choice for the energy slot, but Friday they said she was dropped at the last minute in order to add a Hispanic to the cabinet.
"I'll be damned," said David Luken, a lobbyist for the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities.
"(Pena's) an unknown for the industry," said a natural gas industry official.
At least one environmental group frowned on the choice, recalling Pena's record at the Transportation Department.

"He spent the last several years rolling over to the auto industry on issues from safety to cleaner cars, and having declined to make cars and light trucks more energy efficient, it doesn't necessarily bode well for what he'll do at the Energy Department," said Dan Becker, energy program director for the Sierra Club.
But energy efficiency advocates were more optimistic about Pena, given his background as former mayor of Denver.

"We look back on his record in Denver on energy issues. He did support alternative fuels for vehicles," said Scott Denman, executive director of the Safe Energy Communication Council. "We are anticipating that he will continue the Clinton administration's move toward efficiency, renewables, and sustainable technologies."
David Nemtzow, president of the Alliance to Save Energy, said Pena's experience in dealing with a broad range of policy issues made him a strong choice.
Two-thirds of the Energy Department's budget is devoted to maintenance of U.S. nuclear weapons and cleanup of nuclear waste from former weapons manufacturing plants.

"The most important attributes of the secretary in the nuclear weapons area is going to be openness to all points of view," said Arjun Makhijani, president of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research, adding that it would be counterproductive to second-guess Clinton's decision on Pena.

"It's a very complicated area with a very difficult history and very huge problems from the most global to the most local that will be facing him that are completely disproportionate to the relative size of the budget," he said.
